## Question Information
**Question Description**: Amazing project! A few questions for my specific usecase

Hey guys, I've been lurking on the project for a few weeks now, and I have a few questions. I'm trying to determine of this will do what I want it to do. I'm not looking for an accurate simulation of television, rather for my own take on things.
This is my current setup:
Right now, I have several dumpster dove Raspberry Pis, each with a USB drive of media and a simple yet elegant script to play that media in a random order using a video looper solution (a free, pre-configured software that turns a Raspberry Pi into a dedicated video looping device, playing H.264 MP4 files continuously from a USB stick in alphabetical or random order, with hot-swapping support). Each Pi outputs to an AV switch going into my CRT, and to change the "channel", I just flip to a different input. A little dumb, but it works.
Right now, each USB drive has more or less the same content on it. Currently, I don't have enough content of any logical category to organize my media into specific channels. Eventually, I will but until then I am perfectly okay with this pure chaos. The reason for bothering with multiple channels in the first place is to ensure there's a variety of options to choose from at any given moment. I generally watch at around the same time every day, so if I tried to use fine-tuned scheduling, it would just limit what I see.
I try to curate it in a way that things generally stick to 10 to 20ish minutes long, but durations vary wildly. Everything from a few minutes long PSAs to several hours of raw archival footage. Think the best of nuggets of AV Geeks ephemera, failed pilots, and weird artifacts from decades of Public Access television.
I'm not sure how compatible this is with the philosophy of the project. I foresee attempts to pad things out with commercials and bumpers will result in a very uneven viewing experience.
Because of all of this, I don't see a sane way to utilize proper channels or any semblance of scheduling. If I start using FS42, my first goal is just to recreate what I have now: 3 or 4 channels (or more! ) all pulling from the same chaotic stream of consciousness. No timeslots, tags/scheduling, or commercials.
Eventually, when I DO have a much larger pool of media it would probably make more sense to start having specialized channels, but I think I'll still always want to have at least some chaos channels and to generally play fast and loose with schedules.
Here are my questions:


Can this project actually do what I'm after? Basically, will it "let me" use it in this totally underutilized way, simply having multiple channels, all playing the same pool of random stuff in no real order?


Right now in the old setup, I'm avoiding putting entire shows in my pool because I don't have a good way to prevent an unintentional marathon. Here, is there a good way to say "if you play a video from this folder, don't play another from it for at least X hours"?


Furthermore, as I continue to build my library, does anyone have suggestions for how I should start organizing it? Right now, every video is just chilling in the root of the drive and I am not looking forward to correcting that.

**Answer**: You absolutely can bend FS42 to your use case, though you’ll be using just a subset of what it can do.

Below I’ll break it into your three questions and keep it concrete / practical.

---

## 1. “Chaos channels” with the same pool of random stuff

FS42 is built around “stations” and schedules, but it does not enforce that you use commercials, bumps, or even sophisticated scheduling logic. From the repository docs:

- `station_42.py` is the “Main CLI and UI for building catalogs and schedules` and
- `field_player.py` is the “Main TV interface/player”  
(from `README.md`, lines 71–76)

Stations are defined in JSON under `confs/`, and content is under `catalog/`. The core station manager loads station configs and just treats them as a set of “stations” with attributes like `network_name`, `channel_number`, and `network_type`:

```python
self.stations = sorted(station_configs, key=lambda station: station["channel_number"])
...
for station in self.stations:
    self._name_index[station["network_name"]] = station
    self._number_index[station["channel_number"]] = station
```  
(`fs42/station_manager.py`, lines 183–210)

The main pieces that might get in your way conceptually (commercials, bumps, etc.) are driven by station configuration and scheduling, not hard‑wired behavior in `StationManager`. There’s no requirement in this code that every station must have ads or bumps; stations are just configurations that feed into the rest of the system.

So you can:

- Define several stations (3–4 or more) all pointing at:
  - The same catalog folder, or
  - Overlapping sets of content
- Configure those stations to:
  - Not use commercials or bumps
  - Use “loop”/continuous content behavior rather than “network schedule” style

The exact knobs for “no commercials/bumpers” and “loop” vs “traditional scheduling” live in the station configuration files and the scheduler/catalog code, which isn’t shown in the context here, so I can’t quote the specific JSON keys. But the architecture shown in `StationManager` is perfectly fine with multiple stations that are conceptually “dumb random streams”.

If you’re okay with a tiny amount of structure, a very simple setup that matches your current system is:

- One large “chaos” catalog folder (e.g. `catalog/chaos/`), with all your short clips and weird artifacts.
- 3–4 station configs that each reference that same pool.
- Use FS42’s player to switch “channels” instead of physically switching inputs.

That gets you:

- Multiple channels active at once.
- No strict time slots required.
- No mandatory commercials/bumpers.

You’d mostly be “under‑using” the scheduler instead of fighting it.

---

## 2. “If you play a video from this folder, don’t play another from it for X hours”

FS42 *does* track what has been played recently and tries to avoid repeats, but the precise logic for “cooldowns” isn’t visible in the snippets you provided, and there’s no exposed configuration for “cooldown by folder for X hours” in the visible code.

What we *can* see:

- The project maintains a runtime database: `"db_path": "runtime/fs42_fluid.db"`  
  (`fs42/station_manager.py`, lines 40–47)
- One of the stated design goals is “randomly selects shows that have not been played recently”:
  > “To keep a fresh lineup, randomly selects shows that have not been played recently”  
  (`README.md`, lines 108–111)

So conceptually, FS42 already has an internal idea of “recently played” and tries to space things out. However:

- The code shown does not expose a per‑folder cooldown configuration.
- There’s no obvious config key in `load_main_config` for something like “cooldown hours per folder”. It only handles keys such as `"db_path"`, `"normalize_titles"`, `"tmdb_api_key"`, `"recall_last_channel"`, `"title_patterns"`, and `"day_parts"`.  
  (`fs42/station_manager.py`, lines 116–120, 132–173)

So, with just this context:

- Yes: FS42 *already* tries not to immediately repeat content.
- Unknown: Whether you can say “this folder can only supply one clip per 4 hours” via config alone.

If you eventually want that precise behavior, you’d likely need a (fairly small) code change in whatever module chooses clips (not shown in the snippets) to:

- Tag shows by folder.
- Store “last played time” per folder in the DB.
- Reject candidates from a folder until `now - last_played_folder_time >= X`.

Without that selector code visible, I can’t show you the exact patch, but architecturally it’s compatible with how FS42 already logs and consults play history.

---

## 3. How to start organizing your growing library

You’ll be in a much better place for *both* FS42 and your current Pi‑looper approach if you start gently introducing structure now. A practical strategy that works well with FS42:

### 3.1. Introduce broad “buckets”, not micro‑channels

Instead of dumping everything in one root folder, create very coarse folders that reflect “vibe” rather than precise genres, for example:

- `catalog/chaos/` – anything truly random and short.
- `catalog/longform/` – multi‑hour tapes, raw archival material.
- `catalog/seriesish/` – things that are more like episodic shows.
- `catalog/ads_psa/` – PSAs, interstitials, etc. (even if you *don’t* use them now).

You can absolutely still scatter very different things inside each; the point is only to have *some* levers later:

- Want to reduce accidental marathons? Lower priority for `seriesish` for chaos channels.
- Want to bias late‑night toward truly weird long stuff? Increase weight for `longform` in those hours.

FS42’s scheduler already thinks in terms of day parts:

```python
"day_parts": {
    "morning": range(6, 10),
    "daytime": range(10, 18),
    "prime": range(18, 23),
    "late": [23, 0, 1, 2],
    "overnight": range(2, 6),
},
```  
(`fs42/station_manager.py`, lines 31–38)

And lets you override those via config:  

```python
if "day_parts" in d:
    new_parts = {}
    for key in d["day_parts"]:
        start_hour = d["day_parts"][key]["start_hour"]
        end_hour = d["day_parts"][key]["end_hour"]
        ...
        self.server_conf["day_parts"] = new_parts
```  
(`fs42/station_manager.py`, lines 151–171)

So once your library grows, you can start to say things like “this station pulls mostly from these buckets in prime, those buckets at night”, without rewriting your entire filesystem.

### 3.2. Use decent file names; FS42 is good at parsing them

The project has a fairly robust `TitleParser`:

```python
class TitleParser:
    @staticmethod
    def parse_title(in_str: str, custom_patterns: list = None) -> str:
        ...
        # Default built-in patterns
        default_patterns = [
            ...
            # Title + separators + season/episode pattern
            (r"^(.+?)" + sep + r"(?:[sS]\d+(?:" + sep + r"?[eE]\d+)+ ...", 1),
            ...
            # Just title (fallback)
            (r"^(.+)$", 1),
        ]
        ...
        for pattern, group in patterns:
            match = re.match(pattern, filename)
            if match:
                title = match.group(group)
                ...
                return " ".join(word.capitalize() for word in title.split())
```  
(`fs42/title_parser.py`, lines 5–41, 51–63)

So:

- You don’t need perfect names, but:
  - Avoid everything being `VID001.mp4`, `VID002.mp4`, etc.
  - Put at least a recognizable title upfront:  
    `Cool_Public_Access_Show_S01E02_Something_Weird.mp4`  
    `Weird_PSA_1987-Seat_Belts.mp4`
- If you have oddball naming schemes, you can define `title_patterns` in the main config, and FS42 will load them and apply them *before* its built‑ins:

```python
if "title_patterns" in d:
    ...
    # Add as tuple (pattern, group) to match existing format
    custom_patterns.append((pattern_config["pattern"], pattern_config["group"]))
...
self.server_conf["title_patterns"] = custom_patterns
```  
(`fs42/station_manager.py`, lines 132–168)

Those then get used by `TitleParser.parse_title(custom_patterns=...)`.

This is especially helpful if you have rip sets with weird prefixes or numbering—FS42 can still infer sensible titles.

### 3.3. Plan for both “chaos” and future themed channels

Given your goals, a nice long‑term structure is:

- Keep your current chaos pool as its own top‑level catalog area that can be shared by many stations.
- As you accumulate enough content in a category, *also* duplicate or symlink it into a more specific folder:
  - `catalog/horror/`
  - `catalog/game_shows/`
  - `catalog/local_public_access/`

That way:

- Your chaos stations can continue to point to “everything”.
- Themed stations can point to more specific trees, without you needing to re‑rip or totally reorganize.

FS42 happily mounts multiple directories into the container (if you use Docker), and has explicit `catalog/`, `confs/`, and `runtime/` separation:  

> “The ‘catalog’, ‘confs’, and ‘runtime’ folders are all mounted so that their data will persist across runs of this container.”  
(`docker/README.md`, lines 52–54)

So it’s quite friendly to “evolve” your layout over time.

---

## Putting it together for *your* first step

To recreate your current multi‑Pi chaos:

1. Install FS42 and run it as per README:
   ```bash
   ./install.sh
   python3 station_42.py --rebuild_catalog --schedule
   python3 field_player.py
   ```  
   (`README.md`, lines 21–37)

2. Create:
   - One big `catalog/chaos` directory with your current pool.
   - 3–4 station configs in `confs/` that:
     - All point to that directory.
     - Disable commercials and bumpers (via config—details are in files not shown here, but it’s supported behavior).
     - Don’t try to model strict “shows at 7:00pm” time slots.

3. Use the FS42 player to change channels instead of switching AV inputs. FS42 will:
   - Keep each “channel” playing continuously.
   - Consider play history when picking what’s next (avoiding very tight repeats).

Later, when your library grows, you can:

- Split content into more folders and define new stations.
- Tune scheduling to be looser or tighter by day part.
- If you want a strong “cooldown per folder” rule, add a small custom rule in the selector code (you or a contributor), leveraging the DB at `runtime/fs42_fluid.db` and the “recently played” behavior FS42 already has.

If you describe how your files are currently named and give a rough idea of how you’d like a “chaos” station JSON to look, I can sketch a concrete example station config and a migration plan for your folders.

## Reference Answer
Hey! Thanks for the questions - I think I can help out.

>1. Can this project actually do what I'm after? Basically, will it "let me" use it in this totally underutilized way, simply having multiple channels, all playing the same pool of random stuff in no real order?

Yes. You would just put all your content under a single folder in your content dir, let's call it `random`, then, when you configure the stations, here are the important parts of the settings:

```json
  "network_type": "standard"
  "schedule_increment": 0
```

This will tell it that you don't want commercials or bumps, when one show is over, move on to the next. Then, in the time slots, just set every one over them to this:

```json
"13": {"tags" : "random"}
"14": {"tags" : "random"}
"15": {"tags" : "random"}
```

Then it will pick mostly randomly (giving some preferences to things that haven't played recently) from the content inside the folder called `random` Overall, I think it would work in your use case.

>2 Right now in the old setup, I'm avoiding putting entire shows in my pool because I don't have a good way to prevent an unintentional marathon. Here, is there a good way to say "if you play a video from this folder, don't play another from it for at least X hours"?

When it picks what to play, if all counts are equal, it will choose at random. From there, it will choose randomly from the pool with the lowest play count. There are things you could play with here too with splitting your content up a little into different tags, so you don't pull from the same pool for multiple hours - but then you are making schedules.

>3 Furthermore, as I continue to build my library, does anyone have suggestions for how I should start organizing it? Right now, every video is just chilling in the root of the drive and I am not looking forward to correcting that.

I arrange mine by shows, but then I might group a bunch of different show folders under one directory and just call that `sitcoms` - then, you can use tags to decide how you want to schedule.

This will pull any show under `content_dir/sitcom` (`content_dir` is defined in the station config)

```json
"20": {"tags" : "sitcom"}
```

But if I want a specific show under `sitcom`, I can do this:

```json
"20": {"tags" : "sitcom/ALF"}
```

This will only pull shows from `content_dir/sitcom/ALF`
